title: Saga Pattern
description: Learn the Saga pattern for managing distributed transactions in microservices.

data.text: The Saga pattern is the de facto standard for distributed transactions in microservices. Amazon, Uber, and Netflix all use Saga patterns to manage complex business transactions that span multiple services without blocking or reducing availability.

A Saga is a sequence of local transactions. Each local transaction updates data in one service and publishes an event. If a step fails, compensating transactions undo the previous steps. Unlike 2PC, Sagas never block and provide eventual consistency.

data.title: Orchestration vs Choreography
items: Orchestration: Central coordinator (saga orchestrator) manages the flow
Choreography: Services react to events without central coordination
Orchestration is better for complex flows with many steps
Choreography is simpler for small, decoupled flows

data.title: Compensating Transactions
data.text: Compensating transactions undo the effects of a previous transaction. For example, if Payment succeeds but Shipping fails, the compensating transaction refunds the payment. Compensating transactions must be idempotent.

data.title: Example: Order Saga with Orchestration
data.code: An order saga managed by an orchestrator.

# Order Saga (Orchestration)
# 1. Create Order (Order Service) -> OrderCreated
# 2. Reserve Inventory (Inventory Service) -> InventoryReserved
# 3. Process Payment (Payment Service) -> PaymentProcessed
# 4. Create Shipment (Shipping Service) -> ShipmentCreated
#
# If step 3 fails:
# Compensate: Refund Payment -> PaymentRefunded
# Compensate: Release Inventory -> InventoryReleased
# Compensate: Cancel Order -> OrderCancelled

# If step 4 fails:
# Compensate: Refund Payment
# Compensate: Release Inventory
# Compensate: Cancel Order

data.caption: Saga orchestration flow
data.definition:
graph LR
    O[Order Service] -->|1. Create| I[Inventory Service]
    I -->|2. Reserve| P[Payment Service]
    P -->|3. Process| S[Shipping Service]
    S -->|4. Create| E[End]
    P -.->|Compensate| CR[Refund Payment]
    I -.->|Compensate| RL[Release Inventory]
    O -.->|Compensate| CC[Cancel Order]

items.question: What is the difference between orchestration and choreography?
items.answer: Orchestration uses a central coordinator to manage the flow. Choreography uses events and lets services coordinate themselves. Orchestration is clearer for complex flows; choreography is more decoupled.

items.question: How do I ensure compensating transactions work?
items.answer: Compensating transactions must be idempotent and reliably executed. Use the same reliability patterns (retries, circuit breakers) for compensating transactions as for regular operations.

items.question: What about partial failures during compensation?
items.answer: Use a saga log to track the state. If compensation fails, retry with backoff. If it still fails, alert operators for manual intervention.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Saga is the standard pattern for distributed transactions
Uses local transactions and compensating actions
Choose orchestration for complex flows, choreography for simple ones
data.takeaway: Saga pattern enables distributed transactions while maintaining availability; it is the microservices alternative to 2PC.
